response.title: Do the built-in filters on enclosed 3D printers actually remove ABS fumes, or do I need to vent it out a window?
response.answer:
For printing ABS indoors, I strongly recommend venting your enclosed 3D printer outside through a window. Most built-in filtration systems reduce fumes but don't reliably eliminate them.

The important distinction is that ABS printing produces two types of airborne pollutants:

VOCs (volatile organic compounds): Especially styrene, which can irritate your eyes and respiratory system. Activated carbon can capture some VOCs, but effectiveness varies significantly.

Ultrafine particles (UFPs): Extremely small particles that can penetrate deep into the lungs. HEPA filters can capture these effectively, provided the air actually passes through the filter.

An enclosed printer with a built-in HEPA and carbon filter is better than an unfiltered printer, but it's not necessarily safe for prolonged ABS printing in an occupied room.

How effective are the different approaches?

*Assuming the filter is properly sealed and the airflow is sufficient.

The biggest weakness of many consumer 3D printers is their small activated-carbon filters. A thin carbon sheet or small cartridge may reduce odor without adequately controlling styrene exposure.

Also, an enclosure isn't necessarily airtight. Pollutants can escape through gaps, during door opening, and when removing a freshly printed part.

What I'd recommend for a home setup
Shop

Best: Enclosure + duct + window exhaust

Connect an exhaust duct to the enclosure and use an inline fan to pull fumes outside. Aim for slight negative pressure so leaks draw room air inward rather than release fumes.

Shop

Second choice: Substantial HEPA + activated-carbon filtration

A well-designed, sealed recirculation system with enough carbon and verified performance can meaningfully reduce exposure. I wouldn't assume a small factory-installed filter is sufficient without testing data.

For outdoor exhaust, keep these practical details in mind:

Use a window insert that seals around the duct, not just an open window.

Avoid excessive exhaust airflow while printing ABS because it can cool the chamber and cause warping.

Keep the enclosure closed during printing and allow time for ventilation before opening it.

Discharge away from nearby windows or air intakes, and follow the printer manufacturer's ventilation guidance.

NIOSH recommends ventilated enclosures and local exhaust controls. A NIOSH study found outdoor exhaust among the most effective particle-control methods tested. 
CDC
+1

One question that makes a big difference

Which enclosed 3D printer do you have or plan to buy? For example, a Bambu Lab X1C, P1S, H2D, Qidi, or Creality K1.

The answer matters because some printers have only a small carbon filter, while others have more substantial filtration systems. I can help determine whether your specific printer's built-in filter is adequate for ABS or whether external ventilation is worth installing.
